correctness.summary: The exact coordinate energy decrement reduces the sharp fixed-sampling factor to lambda_min(P^{1/2} C P^{1/2}). For q=C^{-1}1, a Rayleigh test and Cauchy-Schwarz give rho(p)<=1/(1^Tq). At p=q/(1^Tq), nonnegativity of the inverse scaled matrix and a positive eigenvector identify its Perron root, proving equality; Cauchy equality gives uniqueness. The Poisson formulas follow from the closed-form discrete Green response to unit forcing. Deterministic numerical checks reproduce the matrix identities and formulas.

originality.scope: to the best of our knowledge
originality.summary: The checked randomized-coordinate literature gives the general exact-rate optimization through semidefinite programming or optimizes different probability-dependent bounds. The equivalent saturated E-optimal-design literature was also checked, including Pukelsheim-Torsney's general linearly independent support-point theory. Searches under randomized coordinate/Gauss-Seidel, inverse-positive and M-matrix, E-optimal-design, diagonal-scaling and equivalent smallest-eigenvalue formulations did not locate the closed form p proportional to C^{-1}1 for this class. Broad historical optimal-design and matrix-scaling literature remains the principal residual prior-coverage risk.

value.summary: The theorem converts a generic semidefinite probability optimization into a unique explicit formula requiring one linear solve on a natural numerical-linear-algebra class that includes SPD Stieltjes matrices. It also gives an explicit 1D Poisson sampling profile and a quantified sharp-rate improvement over uniform sampling.

limitations: Exact arithmetic and exact single-coordinate minimization only.
Sampling is fixed and iid; adaptive, without-replacement, block, greedy, accelerated, spectral and conjugate-direction rules are outside the theorem.
Optimality concerns the sharp worst-case one-step expected A-energy/objective-gap factor, not every norm or finite-horizon policy.
Computing the optimal distribution for a generic matrix requires a linear solve and therefore is not automatically a cheaper solver.
The inverse-positive condition is sufficient and is not asserted necessary for some other matrix to admit a closed form.
Broad historical optimal-design and diagonal-scaling literature leaves residual originality risk.
Independent audit has not been performed.
